subject: physics
question_text: Show that C_P − C_V = R for an ideal gas, where the symbols have their usual meaning. A Carnot engine works between temperatures 127 °C and 327 °C. Calculate its efficiency.

mark_split.label: Work term from the gas equation

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Long Answer Question 1 (printed p.131). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The eight 1-mark step split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the constant-volume relation ΔQ = C_V ΔT = ΔU, the constant-pressure relation ΔQ = C_P ΔT = ΔU + PΔV, PΔV = RΔT from PV = RT at constant pressure, the substitution reaching C_P − C_V = R for MOLAR specific heats, and the Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 − 400/600 = 1/3 = 33.3% with T₁ = 600 K (327 °C) and T₂ = 400 K (127 °C) all match the standard NCERT Class-11 Chapter 12 (Thermodynamics) treatment.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Constant volume path
lines: For one mole of an ideal gas, at
constant volume no work is done, so
all the heat raises the internal
steps.margin_note: First mark. State constant volume, then ΔQ = C_V ΔT = ΔU.
steps.why: This fixes what C_V means physically: at constant volume every joule of heat supplied becomes internal energy, none of it is spent doing work.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔQ = C_V ΔT without also equating it to ΔU — the equality with ΔU is the whole point of this step.
Forgetting the one mole condition — C_V here is the molar specific heat, not the specific heat per unit mass.

recall.must_convey: That at constant volume, for one mole, ΔQ = C_V ΔT equals ΔU because no work is done.
accept: at constant volume delta Q is C_V delta T
no work is done at constant volume
delta Q equals delta U at constant volume
C_V delta T equals delta U
reject: delta Q equals C_P delta T

steps.memory_tip: Constant volume: no work, so all the heat goes into ΔU.

steps.label: Constant pressure path
lines: At constant pressure the same one
mole also does work PΔV as it
expands, so the heat supplied for
the same rise in temperature is
steps.margin_note: Second mark. ΔQ = C_P ΔT = ΔU + PΔV, for the same ΔT.
steps.why: Comparing the same temperature rise at constant pressure against the constant-volume case is what lets the two heat capacities be subtracted in the next steps.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the PΔV term — at constant pressure the gas does external work, so ΔQ is not just ΔU.
Using a different ΔT for this step — the comparison only works because the SAME temperature rise ΔT is used in both paths.

recall.must_convey: That at constant pressure, for the same ΔT, ΔQ = C_P ΔT equals ΔU plus PΔV.
accept: at constant pressure delta Q is C_P delta T
C_P delta T equals delta U plus P delta V
the gas also does work P delta V
same delta T at constant pressure
reject: delta Q equals C_V delta T

steps.memory_tip: Constant pressure: the gas also pushes outward, so C_P carries an extra PΔV.

steps.label: Work term from the gas equation
lines: For one mole, PV = RT. At constant
steps.margin_note: Third mark. PV = RT at constant pressure gives PΔV = RΔT.
steps.why: PΔV is the work done in the constant-pressure step, and this line turns it into a term written with R — the ingredient the final result needs.
common_mistakes: Applying PV = RT at the wrong step — it is used HERE, at constant pressure, not in the constant-volume step.
Writing VΔP instead of PΔV — pressure is held constant, so it is the volume that changes.

recall.must_convey: That PV = RT at constant pressure gives PΔV = RΔT.
accept: P V equals R T
at constant pressure P delta V equals R delta T
difference the ideal gas equation
P delta V is R delta T

steps.memory_tip: Constant P, so only V changes: PΔV = RΔT falls straight out of PV = RT.

steps.label: The ideal-gas step
lines: For an ideal gas, the internal
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. ΔU depends only on T for an ideal gas, so C_V ΔT from the constant-volume step applies at constant pressure too, for the same ΔT.
steps.why: The first law fixes ΔU for a process, but only for an IDEAL GAS is U a function of temperature alone — that is what lets the SAME ΔU = C_V ΔT, found at constant volume, be reused for the constant-pressure path with the same ΔT.
common_mistakes: Assuming ΔU = C_V ΔT only at constant volume — it holds for ANY process with the same ΔT, because an ideal gas's internal energy depends on temperature alone, not on volume or pressure.
Skipping this reasoning and jumping straight from the constant-pressure equation to the boxed result — the substitution needs this ideal-gas fact stated first.

recall.must_convey: That for an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature alone, so ΔU = C_V ΔT applies with the same ΔT whether the process is at constant volume or constant pressure.
accept: ideal gas internal energy depends only on temperature
delta U equals C_V delta T in any process
same delta U at constant pressure as at constant volume

steps.memory_tip: For an ideal gas, U depends on T alone — the same ΔU = C_V ΔT works at constant volume or pressure.

steps.label: Substitute and solve
lines: C_P and C_V here are the MOLAR
specific heats, for one mole of gas.
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Substitute ΔU = C_V ΔT (from the ideal-gas step) and PΔV = RΔT, then box C_P − C_V = R for molar specific heats.
steps.why: The previous step showed ΔU = C_V ΔT holds for this same ΔT at constant pressure too — substituting that, together with PΔV = RΔT, into the constant-pressure equation turns it into a relation between C_P, C_V and R alone, for one mole.
common_mistakes: Substituting PΔV = RΔT but forgetting to also replace ΔU with C_V ΔT — both substitutions are needed to reach C_P − C_V = R.
Writing C_P − C_V = R next to a per-unit-mass definition of specific heat without noting these are molar quantities.
Leaving R on the wrong side, writing C_V − C_P = R.

recall.must_convey: That substituting ΔU = C_V ΔT and PΔV = RΔT into the constant-pressure equation and dividing by ΔT gives C_P − C_V = R, for molar specific heats.
accept: substitute C_V delta T and R delta T
divide through by delta T
C_P minus C_V equals R
these are molar specific heats
reject: P delta V equals R delta T

steps.memory_tip: Substitute both ΔU = C_V ΔT and PΔV = RΔT into the constant-pressure equation, then divide by ΔT.

steps.label: Convert to kelvin
lines: A Carnot engine works between a
source at 327 °C and a sink at
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Convert both temperatures to kelvin — this is what makes the substitution in the next step possible.
steps.why: The efficiency formula η = 1 − T₂/T₁ only holds for absolute temperature — using the Celsius values directly gives the wrong number, so the complete answer states the conversion explicitly.
common_mistakes: Substituting 327 and 127 directly into η = 1 − T₂/T₁ without converting to kelvin first.
Swapping which temperature is the source and which is the sink — the higher temperature, 600 K, is the source T₁.

recall.must_convey: That the source at 327 degrees Celsius is 600 kelvin and the sink at 127 degrees Celsius is 400 kelvin, converted before using the efficiency formula.
accept: 327 degrees celsius is 600 kelvin
127 degrees celsius is 400 kelvin
convert to kelvin before using the formula
T one is 600 K, T two is 400 K
reject: eta equals one minus T two by T one

steps.memory_tip: Add 273 before anything else: 327 °C is 600 K, 127 °C is 400 K.

steps.label: Apply the efficiency formula
lines: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Write η = 1 − T₂/T₁, then substitute 400 and 600.
steps.why: This is the standard Carnot result — substituting the two absolute temperatures already found is what turns the formula into a number.
common_mistakes: Writing η = T₂/T₁ without the 1 − in front.
Substituting the Celsius values here instead of the kelvin values already found.

recall.must_convey: That efficiency is one minus T two over T one, substituted as one minus 400 over 600.
accept: eta equals one minus T two by T one
one minus 400 by 600
substitute 400 and 600
one minus two thirds
heard_as: one minus T two by T one

steps.memory_tip: η = 1 − T₂/T₁: the sink over the source, subtracted from one.

steps.label: The efficiency
lines: As a decimal and a percentage,
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. Simplify to 1/3 and state 33.3 % as the final answer.
steps.why: The result is worth stating in both forms — the fraction shows where it came from, and the percentage is the number an examiner and a student both recognise as the answer.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the fraction 1/3 — it is already a complete correct answer; the percentage form, 33.3 %, is the conventional way to present it and is worth adding.
Writing 33.3 without the percent sign, which reads as a bare number rather than the efficiency.

recall.must_convey: That one minus two thirds simplifies to one third, which is 33.3 percent, the final efficiency.
accept: one minus two thirds is one third
the efficiency is one third
33.3 percent
reject: one minus T two by T one

steps.memory_tip: 1/3 as a percentage is 33.3 % — the final boxed answer.

insider_note: The complete answer states explicitly that these are MOLAR specific heats, and converts both temperatures to kelvin before substituting.
